title: Maximum Points Inside the Square
statement:
Point `i` sits at `points[i] = [x, y]` and carries the lowercase letter `s[i]` as its tag. You may draw any square whose centre is the origin `(0, 0)` and whose sides run parallel to the axes; its side length can be any value from `0` upwards, and a point lying on the border counts as covered.

A square is allowed only when the points it covers all have different tags. Return the largest number of points that an allowed square can cover (this is `0` when no allowed square covers any point).
constraints: No two points have the same coordinates
s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

A square centred at the origin with half side `d` covers `(x, y)` exactly when `max(|x|, |y|) <= d`. So each point reduces to one number, `dist = max(|x|, |y|)`, and a growing square takes in points in increasing order of `dist`, all points with equal `dist` at once. Sort by `dist` and accept whole groups until a tag repeats. Trying every half side and recounting the covered points also works, but costs O(n²).

## Approach

1. Turn each point into `{ dist, tag }` and sort these by `dist` into `order`.
2. `inside` counts the points of the groups accepted so far (it is also where the next group starts); `seen` holds their tags.
3. Scan the group that shares `order[inside].dist` with `next`.
4. If a point's `tag` is already in `seen` (from an earlier group or earlier in this group), the square must stop just short of this group, so return `inside`.
5. Otherwise add the tag to `seen`; when the group ends, set `inside = next`.
6. If every group fits, every point is covered: return `inside`.

## Example 1, step by step

The distances are `2` (a), `2` (b), `4` (d), `3` (c) and `3` (a), so `order` is (2, a), (2, b), (3, c), (3, a), (4, d). The group at distance 2 adds `a` and `b`, and `inside` becomes 2. In the group at distance 3, `c` is new, but `a` is already in `seen`, so the answer is `2`: the square of side 4 that covers the first two points.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for the sort; the scan visits each point at most once.
- Space: O(n) for `order`; `seen` never holds more than 26 tags.

## Pitfalls

- Border points count as covered, so a square cannot take only some points of one distance group. A repeated tag inside a group blocks the whole group (Example 3): return the count before the group, not the count up to the clashing point.
- Measure with `max(|x|, |y|)`, not the Euclidean distance or `|x| + |y|`: `[3,3]` fits in a square of half side 3, while `[4,0]` needs 4.
- The answer can be `0` (Example 3), and a point at the origin is covered even by the square of side 0.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `order` | every point's `dist` and `tag`, sorted by `dist` |
| `seen` | tags of the points already inside the square |
| `inside` | number of points in the accepted groups, and the index where the next group starts |
| `dist` | the distance shared by the current group |
| `next` | index scanning the current group |
| `tag` | the tag of the point at `next` |

narration.2: Reduce each point to max(|x|, |y|), the smallest half side that covers it, and keep its tag.
narration.3: Sort by that distance, so a growing square takes the points in this order.
narration.4: Tags of the points already inside the square.
narration.5: No point is inside yet; inside is also the index where the next distance group starts.
narration.7: Try to add another group while points remain.
narration.8: Every point at this distance enters the square at the same moment.
narration.10: Stay in the group while the distance is unchanged.
narration.11: Read the tag of this point.
narration.12: Is this tag already used by a covered point or by an earlier point of this group?
narration.13: Yes: the square must stop just short of this group, so only the points already inside count.
narration.15: No: record the tag as used.
narration.16: Move on to the next point of the group.
narration.18: The whole group fits, so all of its points are now inside.
narration.20: Every group fit, so the square can cover all the points.
